claim: Flying squirrels are the only group of gliding mammals with a remarkable diversity and wide geographical range.
source: Flying squirrels are the only group of gliding mammals with a remarkable diversity and wide geographical range.
evidence: This is a general statement about flying squirrels that draws from established scientific knowledge about mammalian diversity and biogeography.

claim: Flying squirrels comprise 52 species in 15 genera.
source: They have been classically regarded as a distinct subfamily among the Sciuridae (McKenna and Bell, 1997; McLaughlin, 1984; Simpson, 1945), and even sometimes considered a separate family derived from a different group than the remaining sciurids (De Bruijn and Ünay, 1989; Forsyth Major, 1893; Mein, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koprowski et al., 2016 in the introduction.

claim: Flying squirrels have a wide geographical distribution across Eurasia and North America.
source: Flying squirrels (Sciurinae, Pteromyini) are the only group of gliding mammals to have achieved a significant diversity (52 species in 15 genera) and wide geographical distribution across Eurasia and North America (Koprowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koprowski et al., 2016.

claim: Flying squirrels have been classically regarded as a distinct subfamily among the Sciuridae.
source: They have been classically regarded as a distinct subfamily among the Sciuridae (McKenna and Bell, 1997; McLaughlin, 1984; Simpson, 1945), and even sometimes considered a separate family derived from a different group than the remaining sciurids (De Bruijn and Ünay, 1989; Forsyth Major, 1893; Mein, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous taxonomic work.

claim: Flying squirrels have sometimes been considered a separate family derived from a different group than the remaining sciurids.
source: They have been classically regarded as a distinct subfamily among the Sciuridae (McKenna and Bell, 1997; McLaughlin, 1984; Simpson, 1945), and even sometimes considered a separate family derived from a different group than the remaining sciurids (De Bruijn and Ünay, 1989; Forsyth Major, 1893; Mein, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Bruijn and Ünay, 1989; Forsyth Major, 1893; Mein, 1970.

claim: Presumed fossil flying squirrels are at least as old as (or maybe even older than) the oldest tree squirrels (36.6 – 35.8 Ma).
source: The fact that presumed fossil flying squirrels are at least as old as (or maybe even older than) the oldest tree squirrels (36.6 – 35.8 Ma) may support the latter hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is based on the fossil record and paleontological data.

claim: Flying squirrels are currently recognized as a monophyletic clade.
source: However, flying squirrels are currently recognized as a monophyletic clade, as supported by a set of synapomorphies in the wrist (Thorington, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thorington, 1984, which describes morphological synapomorphies.

claim: The carpal anatomy of flying squirrels is unique and related to the structures that support the patagium.
source: The carpal anatomy of flying squirrels is unique, being related to the structures that support the patagium and their particular gliding position, which is different from that of all other gliding mammals (Thorington, 1984; Thorington and Darrow, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thorington, 1984 and Thorington and Darrow, 2000.

claim: Molecular phylogenies indicate that flying squirrels are nested within tree squirrels.
source: Molecular phylogenies indicate that flying squirrels (tribe Pteromyini) are nested within tree squirrels (subfamily Sciurinae) and likely diverged as recently as the latest Oligocene–early Miocene (23 ± 2.1 Ma) (Fabre et al., 2012; Mercer and Roth, 2003; Steppan et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to molecular phylogenetic studies.

claim: Flying squirrels likely diverged from tree squirrels as recently as the latest Oligocene–early Miocene (23 ± 2.1 Ma) according to molecular phylogenies.
source: Molecular phylogenies indicate that flying squirrels (tribe Pteromyini) are nested within tree squirrels (subfamily Sciurinae) and likely diverged as recently as the latest Oligocene–early Miocene (23 ± 2.1 Ma) (Fabre et al., 2012; Mercer and Roth, 2003; Steppan et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to molecular phylogenetic studies.

claim: Hesperopetes thoringtoni from the late Eocene (36.6 – 35.8 Ma) of North America has been related to the lineage leading to flying squirrels according to dental morphology.
source: Indeed, one of the earliest sciurids, Hesperopetes thoringtoni from the late Eocene (36.6 – 35.8 Ma) of North America, has been related to the lineage leading to flying squirrels according to dental morphology (Emry and Korth, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Emry and Korth, 2007.

claim: In light of molecular results, it was conceded that Hesperopetes unlikely represented a pteromyin.
source: In the light of molecular results, it was conceded that Hesperopetes unlikely represented a pteromyin and was not assigned to any squirrel subfamily (Emry and Korth, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Emry and Korth, 2007.

claim: Hesperopetes appears to have been closely related to Oligopetes.
source: On the other hand, this genus appears to have been closely related to Oligopetes (Emry and Korth, 2007), an earliest Oligocene (ca. 34 – 31 Ma) purported flying squirrel from Europe and Pakistan (Cuenca Bescós and Canudo, 1992; De Bruijn and Ünay, 1989; Heissig, 1979; Marivaux and Welcomme, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Oligopetes is an earliest Oligocene (ca. 34 – 31 Ma) purported flying squirrel from Europe and Pakistan.
source: On the other hand, this genus appears to have been closely related to Oligopetes (Emry and Korth, 2007), an earliest Oligocene (ca. 34 – 31 Ma) purported flying squirrel from Europe and Pakistan (Cuenca Bescós and Canudo, 1992; De Bruijn and Ünay, 1989; Heissig, 1979; Marivaux and Welcomme, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Dental features commonly used to recognize flying squirrels are not unique but also present in other sciurids.
source: Unfortunately, dental features commonly used to recognize flying squirrels are not unique but also present in other sciurids (Thorington et al., 2005), so it is uncertain if any of the extinct 'flying' squirrels belonged to this group.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thorington et al., 2005.

claim: Postcranial remains show diagnostic characters of the pteromyins.
source: Contrary to dental material, postcranial remains do show diagnostic characters of the pteromyins (Thorington, 1984; Thorington et al., 2005; Thorington and Darrow, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The partial skeleton IPS56468 was recovered at Abocador de Can Mata site ACM/C5-D1 with an estimated age of 11.63 Ma.
source: The described partial skeleton (IPS56468; Figure 1, Videos 1, 3D model in Supplementary file 1) was recovered at Abocador de Can Mata site ACM/C5-D1 (els Hostalets de Pierola, Catalonia, Spain; see Materials and Methods), with an estimated age of 11.63 Ma (Alba et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alba et al., 2017 and describes the fossil material.

claim: The recovered remains comprise more than 80 complete and fragmentary bones including the skull and elements of the fore- and hindlimbs.
source: The recovered remains were found partly articulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and comprise more than 80 complete and fragmentary bones including the skull (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and elements of the fore- and hindlimbs (Figures 2–5, Figure 2, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the fossil material and references to figures and tables.

claim: The specimens are assigned to Miopetaurista neogrivensis based on diagnostic cheek tooth morphology.
source: The specimens are assigned to Miopetaurista neogrivensis based on diagnostic cheek tooth morphology (Figure 3; for detailed description and comparisons of cheek teeth morphology see Appendix 3.1).
evidence: This claim is based on morphological analysis of the fossil material.

claim: Miopetaurista neogrivensis has only been reported from La Grive L5 and L3 in France, from Bellestar in Catalonia, and from several sites from the Vallès-Penedès Basin.
source: Miopetaurista neogrivensis has only been reported from La Grive L5 (type locality) and L3 in France, from Bellestar (Seu d'Urgell Basin, also in Catalonia), and from several sites from the Vallès-Penedès Basin (Casanovas-Vilar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Casanovas-Vilar et al., 2015.

claim: The pisiform of M. neogrivensis displays an elevated process for the articulation with the scapholunate, which is characteristic of pteromyins.
source: The pisiform of M. neogrivensis displays an elevated process for the articulation with the scapholunate (Figure 4 and Video 2). This is characteristic of pteromyins, serving as a stabilizer of the styliform cartilage, whereas in other squirrels this bone articulates only with the triquetrum and the distal end of the ulna.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological analysis of the fossil material and comparison with extant forms.

claim: The proximal wrist joint morphology of M. neogrivensis indicates that this species belongs to the pteromyin clade and provides the oldest evidence of gliding locomotion in sciurids.
source: Therefore, the proximal wrist joint morphology of M. neogrivensis indicates that this species belongs to the pteromyin clade and provides the oldest evidence of gliding locomotion in sciurids (see also Appendix 3.3).
evidence: This claim is based on morphological analysis and inference from the fossil material.

claim: M. neogrivensis shares postcranial adaptations with extant pteromyins including elongated and slender limb bones with reduced muscular attachments.
source: The latter is further confirmed by other postcranial adaptations shared with extant pteromyins (Thorington et al., 2005), including the elongated and slender limb bones with reduced muscular attachments (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which enhance joint extension during gliding (Thorington et al., 2005), as well as the elongated lumbar vertebrae (Figure 2; see Appendix 3.3 for a detailed description and comparisons of the postcranial elements).
evidence: This claim is based on morphological analysis and comparison with extant forms, supported by citation.

claim: Body mass of M. neogrivensis was estimated to be 1339 g with 50% confidence intervals of 1116 – 1606 g.
source: Body mass was estimated by means of an allometric regression of body mass vs. skull length in extant sciurids (see Materials and Methods), resulting in 1339 g (50% confidence intervals 1116 – 1606 g thus being in the range of most species of the extant giant flying squirrel Petaurista (about 1200 – 2000 g; Thorington et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on allometric analysis of the fossil material.

claim: The estimated body mass of M. neogrivensis is in the range of most species of the extant giant flying squirrel Petaurista (about 1200 – 2000 g).
source: Body mass was estimated by means of an allometric regression of body mass vs. skull length in extant sciurids (see Materials and Methods), resulting in 1339 g (50% confidence intervals 1116 – 1606 g thus being in the range of most species of the extant giant flying squirrel Petaurista (about 1200 – 2000 g; Thorington et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with extant species, supported by citation.

claim: The pisiform of M. neogrivensis displays a distinct spur (triquetral process) that fits between the palmar surfaces of the scapholunate and the triquetrum.
source: The proximal carpal bones of M. neogrivensis not only unambiguously indicate that it is a flying squirrel, but also allow assigning it to the Pteromyina (Figure 4 and Video 2). The pisiform displays a distinct spur (triquetral process) that fits between the palmar surfaces of the scapholunate and the triquetrum.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological analysis of the fossil material.

claim: The triquetral process is completely lacking in the Glaucomyina.
source: This process is completely lacking in the Glaucomyina (Thorington et al., 2002; Thorington and Darrow, 2000) (Figure 4 and Video 2; see also Appendix 3.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and comparison with extant forms.

claim: The phylogenetic analysis strongly supports M. neogrivensis as the sister taxon of the Petaurista spp. clade.
source: Our analysis strongly supports M. neogrivensis as the sister taxon of the Petaurista spp. clade and indicates a divergence date between flying and tree squirrels ranging from the late Eocene to the late Oligocene (95% highest posterior density [HPD] interval 36.5 – 24.9 Ma; Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analysis combining morphological and molecular data.

claim: The divergence date between flying and tree squirrels ranges from the late Eocene to the late Oligocene (95% HPD interval 36.5 – 24.9 Ma) according to total evidence analysis.
source: Our analysis strongly supports M. neogrivensis as the sister taxon of the Petaurista spp. clade and indicates a divergence date between flying and tree squirrels ranging from the late Eocene to the late Oligocene (95% highest posterior density [HPD] interval 36.5 – 24.9 Ma; Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The Pteromyina and Glaucomyina would have diverged between the late Oligocene–early Miocene (HPD interval 27.1 – 18.1 Ma).
source: The Pteromyina and Glaucomyina would have diverged between the late Oligocene–early Miocene (HPD interval 27.1 – 18.1 Ma; Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The age range for the Sciurini/Pteromyini split spans from the mid Oligocene to early Miocene (HPD interval 30.6 – 17.4 Ma) according to node dating analysis.
source: The age range for the Sciurini/Pteromyini split spans from the mid Oligocene to early Miocene (HPD interval 30.6 – 17.4 Ma; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on node dating phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Divergence estimates derived using independent methods overlap for the late Oligocene.
source: Therefore, divergence estimates derived using independent methods overlap for the late Oligocene.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of results from two different phylogenetic methods.

claim: The two independent phylogenetic analyses estimate divergence dates ranging from 36.5 to 17.4 Ma (late Eocene–early Miocene).
source: The two independent phylogenetic analyses estimate divergence dates ranging from 36.5 to 17.4 Ma (late Eocene–early Miocene; Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Total evidence analysis provides older estimates (36.5 – 24.9 Ma) than node dating (30.6 – 17.4 Ma).
source: Total evidence analysis in particular provides older estimates (36.5 – 24.9 Ma) than node dating (30.6 – 17.4 Ma), but these still marginally overlap with those of previous molecular results.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of results from two different phylogenetic methods.

claim: The late Oligocene should be considered the most likely time for pteromyin divergence.
source: Although allowing for older and younger ages, the independently derived estimates are generally older than previous molecular results (Mercer and Roth, 2003) and overlap for the late Oligocene, which should be considered the most likely time for pteromyin divergence.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Miopetaurista neogrivensis is the oldest unquestionable flying squirrel and dates back to the middle/late Miocene boundary (11.6 Ma).
source: Miopetaurista neogrivensis is the oldest unquestionable flying squirrel and dates back to the middle/late Miocene boundary (11.6 Ma).
evidence: This claim is based on the fossil material and its dating.

claim: The diagnostic wrist anatomy of M. neogrivensis indicates that the two subtribes of flying squirrels had already diverged at 11.6 Ma.
source: Its diagnostic wrist anatomy indicates that the two subtribes of flying squirrels had already diverged at that time.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological analysis and inference from the fossil material.

claim: Flying squirrels experienced little morphological change for almost 12 million years.
source: They also show that flying squirrels experienced little morphological change for almost 12 million years.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of fossil and extant forms.

claim: The ACM composite series ranges from ca. 12.6 to 11.5 Ma.
source: The ACM composite series ranges from ca. 12.6 to 11.5 Ma, the age of the paleontological localities being well constrained thanks to high-resolution litho-, bio- and magnetostratigraphical data (Alba et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alba et al., 2017.

claim: ACM/C5-D1 is correlated to chron C5r.2n (11.657 – 11.592 Ma).
source: ACM/C5-D1 is correlated to chron C5r.2n (11.657 – 11.592 Ma) (Alba et al., 2017), and its interpolated age is 11.64 Ma (Alba et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alba et al., 2017.

claim: The interpolated age of ACM/C5-D1 is 11.64 Ma.
source: ACM/C5-D1 is correlated to chron C5r.2n (11.657 – 11.592 Ma) (Alba et al., 2017), and its interpolated age is 11.64 Ma (Alba et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alba et al., 2017.

claim: Miopetaurista and Pliopetaurista are widely distributed in Europe during the middle and beginning of the late Miocene.
source: In addition, certain genera such as Miopetaurista, Pliopetaurista and Albanensia, are widely distributed (Casanovas-Vilar et al., 2015) (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Casanovas-Vilar et al., 2015.

claim: Most extant Asian flying squirrel genera diverged during the interval from 15 to 10 Ma according to phylogenetic analyses.
source: Our phylogenetic analyses show that most extant Asian flying squirrel genera diverged during the interval from 15 to 10 Ma (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), thus coinciding with this time of high diversity and geographic range extension.
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The skeletons of Miopetaurista and Petaurista show little differences.
source: Perhaps not surprisingly, the skeletons of both genera show little differences.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological comparison of fossil and extant forms.

claim: Sciurids are often regarded as a morphologically conservative group.
source: Sciurids are often regarded as a morphologically conservative group and flying squirrels are no exception having experienced few morphological changes for almost 12 million years.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about sciurid evolution.

claim: Flying squirrels have experienced few morphological changes for almost 12 million years.
source: Sciurids are often regarded as a morphologically conservative group and flying squirrels are no exception having experienced few morphological changes for almost 12 million years.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of fossil and extant forms.

claim: The cheek teeth of Miopetaurista show a simple occlusal pattern, with enamel wrinkling only in the lower molars and no additional lophules.
source: The cheek teeth of Miopetaurista show a simple occlusal pattern, with enamel wrinkling only in the lower molars and no additional lophules (Figure 3, Appendix 3.1).
evidence: This claim is based on morphological analysis of the fossil material.

claim: The dental pattern of Miopetaurista clearly differs from the more complex one of other large-sized flying squirrels, such as Aeretes and Petaurista.
source: This pattern clearly differs from the more complex one of other large-sized flying squirrels, such as Aeretes and Petaurista (Mein, 1970; Thorington et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is based on morphological comparison, supported by citations.

claim: Dental characters, although useful to diagnose the different species and genera, should not warrant high consideration for disentangling the phylogenetic relationships between flying squirrels.
source: This clearly illustrates that dental characters, although useful to diagnose the different species and genera, should not warrant high consideration for disentangling the phylogenetic relationships between flying squirrels.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic results and morphological analysis.

claim: The styliform cartilage, which supports the patagium in all members of the group, attaches to the pisiform and is extended when the wrist is radially abducted and dorsiflexed.
source: The styliform cartilage, which supports the patagium in all members of the group, attaches to the pisiform and is extended when the wrist is radially abducted and dorsiflexed (Thorington, 1984; Thorington and Darrow, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the scapholunate of M. neogrivensis, the articular surface for the radius is much more convex than in tree squirrels, thus resembling the flying squirrel condition.
source: Moreover, in the scapholunate of M. neogrivensis, the articular surface for the radius is much more convex than in tree squirrels, thus resembling the flying squirrel condition, which enables a greater radial abduction.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological analysis and comparison with extant forms.

claim: The elongation of lumbar vertebrae and limbs determines the size and shape of the patagium and dictates important aerodynamic features, such as the decreased wing loading of flying squirrels.
source: The elongation of lumbar vertebrae and limbs determines the size and shape of the patagium and dictates important aerodynamic features, such as the decreased wing loading of flying squirrels (Thorington and Heaney, 1981; Thorington and Santana, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Flying squirrels are divided into two distinct subtribes: Pteromyina, comprising large-sized forms, and Glaucomyina, for the small-sized ones.
source: Based on morphological (Thorington et al., 2002) and molecular data (Mercer and Roth, 2003), flying squirrels are divided into two distinct subtribes: Pteromyina, comprising large-sized forms, and Glaucomyina, for the small-sized ones (Thorington and Hoffmann, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The skull of M. neogrivensis is strikingly similar in size and morphology to that of the other large-sized flying squirrels, particularly Aeromys and Petaurista.
source: The skull, which was virtually reconstructed from two well-preserved specimens (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1-2, Video 3, Table 3), is strikingly similar in size and morphology to that of the other large-sized flying squirrels, particularly Aeromys and Petaurista (for a detailed morphological description of the skull and comparisons see Appendix 3.2).
evidence: This claim is based on morphological analysis and comparison with extant forms.

claim: In the Glaucomyina the tibiocarpalis originates from a tuberosity on the distal tibia which is lacking in M. neogrivensis and the Pteromyina.
source: In the Glaucomyina the tibiocarpalis originates from a tuberosity on the distal tibia which is lacking in M. neogrivensis and the Pteromyina (Thorington et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is based on morphological comparison, supported by citation.

claim: In the Pteromyina, the tibiocarpalis originates from the metatarsals.
source: In the latter, the tibiocarpalis originates from the metatarsals instead.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological knowledge of extant forms.

claim: The broad ranges of divergence estimates are congruent with a previous molecular phylogenetic analysis of the sciurids which placed the split between tree and flying squirrels near the Oligocene/Miocene boundary (23 ± 2.1 Ma).
source: These broad ranges are congruent with a previous molecular phylogenetic analysis of the sciurids (Mercer and Roth, 2003), which placed the split between tree and flying squirrels near the Oligocene/Miocene boundary (23 ± 2.1 Ma), although allowing for substantially older dates.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mercer and Roth, 2003.

claim: Total evidence 95% HPD interval for the pteromyin divergence is consistent with the range of Oligopetes, the oldest records of Sciurion and even the earliest (late Eocene) occurrences of Hesperopetes.
source: Total evidence 95% highest posterior density (HPD) interval for the pteromyin divergence is very broad (36.5–24.9 Ma; Figure 7), being consistent with the range of Oligopetes (Cuenca Bescós and Canudo, 1992; De Bruijn and Ünay, 1989; Heissig, 1979; Marivaux and Welcomme, 2003), the oldest records of Sciurion (Bell, 2004) and even the earliest (late Eocene) occurrences of Hesperopetes (Korth, 2017) (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of phylogenetic results with the fossil record, supported by citations.

claim: Initial flying squirrel diversification and dispersal across the Northern Hemisphere coincided with a period of high mean global temperatures during the early Miocene that peaked between 17 to 15 Ma, during the so-called Mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum.
source: Initial flying squirrel diversification and dispersal across the Northern Hemisphere coincided with a period of high mean global temperatures during the early Miocene that peaked between 17 to 15 Ma, during the so-called Mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum (Zachos et al., 2001) (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zachos et al., 2001.

claim: Humid warm-temperate broadleaf and mixed forests, resembling those existing in the southeastern coast of Asia, characterized the mid latitudes in Eurasia and North America during the early Miocene.
source: Humid warm-temperate broadleaf and mixed forests, resembling those existing in the southeastern coast of Asia, characterized the mid latitudes in Eurasia and North America (Pound et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pound et al., 2012.

claim: Some extant genera, such as Petaurista, Pteromys and Glaucomys, diverged approximately during the Mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum according to phylogenetic analyses.
source: Our phylogenetic analyses show that some extant genera, such as Petaurista, Pteromys and Glaucomys, diverged approximately at that time (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), thus agreeing with previous molecular results (Arbogast et al., 2017; Mercer and Roth, 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analyses, supported by citations.

claim: The warm early Miocene phase was followed by a gradual cooling and the reestablishment of permanent major ice sheets on Antarctica by about 10 Ma.
source: The warm early Miocene phase was followed by a gradual cooling and the reestablishment of permanent major ice sheets on Antarctica by about 10 Ma (Zachos et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zachos et al., 2001.

claim: Most extant species of Petaurista had already diverged during the Pliocene and some even at the latest Miocene according to phylogenetic results.
source: This is again congruent with our results, which show that most extant species had already diverged during the Pliocene and some even at the latest Miocene (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Miopetaurista is remarkably similar to Petaurista, to the point that their postcranial skeleton is virtually identical.
source: It is worth noting that Miopetaurista is remarkably similar to Petaurista, to the point that their postcranial skeleton is virtually identical, even in specificities such as the more reduced lateral epicondylar ridge of the humerus or the wider patellar groove in the femur as compared to other (generally smaller) flying squirrels (for more detailed comparisons see Appendix 3.3).
evidence: This claim is based on morphological comparison of fossil and extant forms.

claim: Large-sized flying squirrels must be regarded as a very conservative group, having experienced little morphological changes since the late middle Miocene.
source: Dental morphological differences apart, it is worth noting that large-sized flying squirrels must be regarded as a very conservative group, having experienced little morphological changes since the late middle Miocene.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from morphological comparison of fossil and extant forms.

claim: Flying squirrels are diverse in the tropical and subtropical forests of the Indo-Malayan region, which apparently acted both as refugia and diversification center since the late Miocene.
source: In contrast, flying squirrels are diverse in the tropical and subtropical forests of the Indo-Malayan region, which apparently acted both as refugia and diversification center (also for tree squirrels) since the late Miocene (Lu et al., 2013; Mercer and Roth, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.
